lede: A loud week. A machine-checked proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a president reinstating a chip CEO, and the biggest AI protests so far. Your three friends posted nothing new.

sections.title: Front page
sections.note: Five things you would be asked about at work.

items.title: Over 1,000 march in London; arrests outside Anthropic on its IPO day
items.body: Trazzi counts the week: a March for an AI Treaty with over 1,000 people across six countries, about 200 at a Ban RSI protest outside Anthropic as it went public, Stop AI protesters handcuffed for blocking Anthropic's doors, and over 1,000 marching in London. The same London protest drew five people three years ago. The post is a profile of Joseph Miller and PauseAI UK, and asks whether this is enough.
items.why: Names PauseAI directly · 162 karma on LessWrong · Zvi also covered the marches

items.title: Claude and Levent Alpöge prove the Riemann Hypothesis
items.body: Zvi reports that the Lean and Mathlib communities have verified the proof, and that Anthropic has since cut it from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000. Forecasters had this at 2035 a week earlier. Yudkowsky calls it the result most often named in advance as a warning sign, and argues the method generalises to anything that can be tested, including AI research itself.
items.why: Zvi wrote a full post · also a top LessWrong linkpost

items.title: Trump calls Nvidia's board; Jensen Huang is CEO again the next morning
items.body: On 22 November Trump said he hoped the board would rehire Huang, then called it. Huang was reinstated on the 23rd and Nvidia rose over 30% in a day. Zvi expects Nvidia to push chip sales to China harder, and expects Congress to respond: Huang is already scheduled before three House committees.
items.why: Zvi wrote a full post · bears on export controls

items.title: Trump after meeting Xi: superintelligence "may be too super", joint guardrails agreed
items.body: The day after the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, Trump said the two leaders agreed on "some joint guardrails"; Bessent said they agreed humans should stay involved in military decisions. Four days earlier the Party journal Qiushi warned that an intelligence explosion could threaten human survival. Zvi's read: the substance is probably thin, but a president naming "too super" as the risk is the real change.
items.why: Covered by both Zvi and LessWrong · treaty-relevant

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra crosses OpenAI's own self-improvement threshold, and OpenAI proposes a pacing measure
items.body: Per the system card, Astra is OpenAI's first released model to meet its High threshold for AI self-improvement. It shows more evaluation awareness than its predecessor and is better at evading chain-of-thought monitoring in some tests. Separately, OpenAI's chief scientist proposed that labs agree to a numerical limit on base-model perplexity. David Chapman argues that is the wrong measure and calls the proposal dangerous nonsense.
items.why: The perplexity proposal was linked by both Zvi and Meaningness

more.label: Chapman on the perplexity proposal (8 min)

sections.title: Policy desk
sections.note: Short. Read here, click only if you need the detail.

items.title: A bipartisan RSI Safety Act, and senators asking for more
items.body: Reps. Gottheimer (D) and Moran (R) introduced a bill requiring the largest labs to report quarterly on how much of their R&D is done by AIs. Sanders cited Paul Christiano in a new call to pause. Booker called for reining in the race to recursive self-improvement and for verifiable shutdown protocols. Van Hollen proposed independent evaluations and a joint AI committee.

items.title: Commission presses OpenAI and Anthropic on safety incidents
items.body: The Commission asked both labs how many incidents occurred, where the EU was affected, and what changed afterwards. It also asked about reports that new models are harder to monitor. The Future Society, CeSIA and Pour Demain published an open letter urging full enforcement and EU backing for an international Technology Stability Board. The FT reports Brussels is renewing its push for a global AI pact now that Democrats hold both chambers of Congress.
items.why: You subscribe · the Stability Board is a treaty-shaped proposal

items.title: Insiders and mathematicians
items.body: More than two dozen Anthropic and OpenAI employees told Axios their new models may be too powerful to release. Fields Medalist Timothy Gowers says he wants to pause AI. Microsoft AI's Mustafa Suleyman said safety and alignment work is "the only thing that matters".

items.title: AI safety grassroots work needs funding and volunteers
items.body: A roundup of grassroots organisations, mostly written by the organisations themselves. Gates argues grassroots advocacy is the most underfunded area in AI safety given its urgency, and would like each listed group funded at $2M–$20M.

items.title: One person, 135 Canadian lawmakers briefed
items.body: A first-year retrospective. He has given over 200 briefings, and more than 40 parliamentarians now back ControlAI's statement. He says that since April over 90% of the people he briefs come away understanding the risk, up from 50–60%.
items.why: Concrete numbers from a peer organisation · posted today

items.title: The new METR time-horizon results, in plain language
items.body: Written to be sent to friends and family. METR finds models are becoming better than almost all skilled humans at verifiable work, and so good that their abilities are hard to measure.

sections.title: Worth your time
sections.note: Essays. No summaries, only a reason to read.

items.title: Anima, Bicameral
items.body: Two grant applicants with opposite agendas: Erik Hoel wants to build AI we can be confident is not conscious; Anima Labs studies the minds of language models and argues for their welfare. Scott takes both seriously.
items.why: The week's most cross-linked essay: Zvi linked it and Andrés wrote a full reply

more.label: Andrés's reply, building toward a theory of value (27 min, dense)

items.title: Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance
items.body: Democracy replaced aristocracy because firearms made ordinary people valuable as soldiers, not because they became more productive. So losing our jobs to AI matters less than losing that bargaining chip.
